title: Combine the two Git state conditions with `and` to determine if the working tree is clean
reading_goal: Use `and` to combine the two "no changes" conditions and interpret the actual meaning of "working tree clean."
question: When this conditional expression evaluates to True, which of the following best describes Git’s `working tree clean` command?
choices: There are no tracked changes or general untracked files to commit within the current review scope.
Even ignored files were all deleted from disk.
It is guaranteed that the remote GitHub server is completely identical in real time.
There have been no commits to this branch yet.
answer: There are no tracked changes or general untracked files to commit within the current review scope.
explanation: Since both tracked and untracked changes are 0, both comparisons evaluate to True, and the result of the "and" operation is also True. Ignored files and remote real-time status are separate issues.
project_context: This connects to the workflow of checking `git status` after making changes to ensure there are no remaining changes before committing.
reading_goal_internal: 추적 변경과 untracked 파일이 모두 0이라는 두 조건이 동시에 참일 때 working tree clean으로 판정하는 논리 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `and` is a logical operator that evaluates to True only when both the left and right conditions are true.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Compare each category corresponding to the changes to be committed in the Git state separately, then combine the two Booleans.
concept_explanation.key_point: "Working tree clean" means there are no tracked changes or general untracked items to commit; it does not necessarily mean that there are no ignored files or that the remote server’s status is identical in real time.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think the repository is clean when only one change count is 0, or to include ignored-file counts in the clean-state decision.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Although the tracked condition is True, the untracked condition is False, so the result of the "and" operation is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `tracked_changes == 0` is True. 2) `untracked_files == 0` is also True. 3) True and True is True. 4) Therefore, the state is determined to be “clean,” with no changes to commit.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the conditions for both commit categories are satisfied simultaneously.

common_wrong_choice.choice: It is guaranteed that the remote GitHub server is completely identical in real time.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The "working tree" status refers to the local working tree and does not guarantee that it is up to date with the remote server.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Separate the local working tree state from the remote synchronization state.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The "Git clean" determination is interpreted as **checking each change category → calculating Boolean conditions → verifying that all are satisfied with an "and" operator**.

title: Modeling Two Types of Git Change States Sequentially Using List Literals
reading_goal: It interprets the structure where the two strings inside the square brackets are separate list items, and “untracked” is the second item.
question: What is the result of `statuses[1]`?
explanation: 1) The first string inside the square brackets is "unstaged." 2) The second string is "untracked." 3) Python list indices start at 0. 4) Therefore, index 1 returns "untracked."
project_context: This connects to the conceptual model in Git that distinguishes between new (untracked) files and changes that have been modified but not yet staged (unstaged) as separate states.
reading_goal_internal: 대괄호 안 두 문자열이 각각 독립된 list 항목이며 untracked가 두 번째 항목이라는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A list literal, in the form `[value1, value2, ...]`, combines multiple values into a single list object in the order they are written.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Find the boundaries of the square brackets and map the actual values, separated by commas, to indices 0 and 1 from the left.
concept_explanation.key_point: For `statuses`, index 0 is `unstaged` and index 1 is `untracked`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to misinterpret the two terms as aliases for the same state or to read the comma as a character within a single string.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the second item is `new`, the result of the index 1 lookup is `new`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The first string inside the square brackets is "unstaged." 2) The second string is "untracked." 3) Python list indices start at 0. 4) Therefore, index 1 returns "untracked."
answer_explanation.why_correct: In the order in which they were written, "untracked" is the second item, and its index is 1.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `unstaged` is the first item at index 0.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Assign indices starting from 0 based on the actual order of the values.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A list literal is read as **separate items → maintain the order in which they are written → correspond to 0-based indices**.

title: Adding a file to the staging list by calling `append()`
reading_goal: Treat the staged list to the left of the dot as the target object, “append” as the method name, and the string to be added as the argument, and read the sequence of state changes.
question: How many items are there in `staged` after the `append` call?
explanation: 1) `staged` starts as an empty list. 2) It looks for the `append` method on the `staged` object. 3) It calls the method, passing the string `new_lesson.json` as an argument. 4) One item is added to the end of the list, so `len(staged)` becomes 1.
project_context: In actual Git, “add” means that changes are prepared in the staging area; here, only that state transition has been modeled as a safe Python list.
reading_goal_internal: 점 왼쪽 staged list를 대상 객체로, append를 메서드 이름으로, 문자열을 추가할 인자로 구분해 상태가 바뀌는 순서를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `list.append(value)` is a method call that adds a single value to the end of the target list and modifies the list itself.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check in the following order: target object → method name → arguments → object state after the call.
concept_explanation.key_point: One item, `new_lesson.json`, is added to the empty `staged` list, bringing its length to 1.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Do not assume that `append` returns a new list, nor should you assume that this example actually modifies the Git index.

teaching_example.walkthrough: `append` adds an item to the queue itself, bringing its length to 1.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `staged` starts as an empty list. 2) It looks for the `append` method on the `staged` object. 3) It calls the method, passing the string `new_lesson.json` as an argument. 4) One item is added to the end of the list, so `len(staged)` becomes 1.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `append` added a single value to the empty list, the number of items increased from 0 to 1.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since `append` directly modifies the target list, it does not remain empty.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Check the state of the target object after the call, rather than the method’s return value.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read a method call as **target object → method → arguments → post-call state/return value**.

title: Passing the commit description string as a keyword argument to ``message=``
reading_goal: Understand the difference in roles: the parameter names inside the function call parentheses are the names of the parameters that `message` will receive, while the string on the right is the actual value passed to it.
question: What is the value of `commit['message']` after calling `make_commit`?
explanation: 1) The `message=` in the call specifies the parameter name that will receive the value. 2) It evaluates the string on the right, “Add Git workflow reading cards.” 3) That string is passed to the `message` parameter of `make_commit`. 4) Since the function returns that same string stored in a dictionary, the query result is also that message.
project_context: In an actual Git commit, a message describing the purpose of the change is required; here, only the structure of that message has been safely modeled as a Python function call.
reading_goal_internal: 함수 호출 괄호 안에서 message가 받을 매개변수 이름이고 오른쪽 문자열이 실제 전달값이라는 역할 차이를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A keyword argument specifies the name of a parameter to be passed in a function call in the form `parameter=value`.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Separate the name on the left of `=` from the expression on the right, evaluate the right-hand value, and pass it to the parameter with that name.
concept_explanation.key_point: The `message` parameter is passed the string "Add Git workflow reading cards."
concept_explanation.common_mistake: You should not assume that `message` is a new global variable assignment or that an actual `git commit` is executed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: `message=` in the call passes the string on the right to the parameter with the same name.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The `message=` in the call specifies the parameter name that will receive the value. 2) It evaluates the string on the right, “Add Git workflow reading cards.” 3) That string is passed to the `message` parameter of `make_commit`. 4) Since the function returns that same string stored in a dictionary, the query result is also that message.
answer_explanation.why_correct: keyword argument Because the string on the right is passed directly to the `message` parameter.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: "message" is the parameter name, and the actual runtime value is the long string on the right.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Separate keywords and their arguments using the equals sign.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read a keyword argument as **identify parameter name → evaluate right-hand value → pass by name**.

title: Comparing whether local and remote branch SHAs match
reading_goal: In a structured branch state, the local and remote SHAs are queried separately, and synchronization is determined based on equality.
question: `synced` What value is stored in ?
explanation: Both dictionary lookups return `def5678`. Since they compare identical strings, the result is True. This is because they compare the identical SHA strings using `==`. A common source of confusion: def5678: That value is the operand of the comparison, and the overall result of the target is a boolean. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the value before the comparison and the comparison result are not distinguished. To determine synchronization, read in the following order: **check both state values → perform equality comparison → obtain boolean result**.
project_context: It is integrated with a CI/CD workflow that uses a status check to verify whether the remote branch points to the intended commit after a `push`.
reading_goal_internal: 구조화된 branch 상태에서 local과 remote SHA를 각각 조회하고 equality로 동기화 여부를 판정한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a == b` compares whether two values are the same. When used with a dict subscription, it first reads the value for each key and then compares the results.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It retrieves the local SHA on the left and the remote SHA on the right, then checks whether the entire string matches.
concept_explanation.key_point: The "Git push" refers to the context of code coverage, while the focus of the Python syntax is on comparing the equality of the two branch state values.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `main -> main` Git output itself is easy to read, much like Python syntax. Here, we focus only on comparing values whose meanings have been structured.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Because the two SHA strings are equal, `synced` is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Both dictionary lookups return `def5678`. Since they compare the same strings, the result is True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because it compares the same SHA strings using `==`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That value is the operand in the comparison, and the result of the entire `target` is a boolean.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the value before the comparison and the result of the comparison are not distinguished.

answer_explanation.takeaway: To determine whether synchronization has occurred, read the sequence: **check both state values → compare for equality → boolean result**.

title: [:7] Creating a short commit hash using `slice`
reading_goal: Using the "stop-exclusion" rule for string slicing, extract the first 7 characters of the entire commit SHA.
question: What is the string stored in `short_hash`?
explanation: A slice retrieves characters from the start up to but not including the `stop` position. Therefore, the first seven characters, `0998190`, are the result. This is because the `stop` boundary is not included in the result of a Python slice. A common source of confusion: 0998190a. This value has eight characters, but `[:7]` retrieves only seven. Point of confusion: This occurs when the stop is mistakenly interpreted as being included. `text[:n]` retrieves the **first n characters**.
project_context: This relates to the notation used to display long commit SHAs as short values in logs and checkpoints.
reading_goal_internal: 문자열 slice의 stop 제외 규칙으로 전체 commit SHA의 앞 7글자를 추출한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `text[:7]` is a slice that takes characters from the start of the string up to, but not including, index 7.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Since there is no "start," it is interpreted as starting at 0 and excluding stop 7.
concept_explanation.key_point: The Git short hash is in the context of code coverage, and the Python syntax focus is on string slicing.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that 8 characters are produced, including the 7th stop. The stop in `slice` is excluded.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The six-character string `abcdef`, with indices ranging from 0 to 5, is selected.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `slice` retrieves the characters from the beginning up to just before `stop 7`. Therefore, the result is the first seven characters: ``0998190``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the stop boundaries of a Python slice are not included in the result.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That value is eight characters long, but `[:7]` takes only seven characters.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where "stop" was interpreted as being included.

title: Find unexpected changes in the diff summary using `in`
reading_goal: A membership test is used to determine whether a specific string is actually included in the list of changes.
question: `has_debug_change` What value is stored in it?
explanation: The search string ``debug=True`` exists as exactly one item in the list. Therefore, the membership test returns `True`. This is because ``in`` returns `True` if the same value exists in the collection. A common source of confusion: `False`—the second item in the list is exactly the same as the search string. Common Misreading: This occurs when the reader does not check all items in the list. If you structure the diff check, you can read it in the following order: **value to find → search the list → boolean result**.
project_context: This ties into the process of reviewing the list of changes just before committing to check for any mixed-in debug settings or unnecessary modifications.
reading_goal_internal: 변경 목록 안에 특정 문자열이 실제로 포함되어 있는지 membership test로 판정한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `value in collection` checks whether the same value exists in the collection and returns a Boolean result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It precisely compares the search string with the list items and returns "True" if they match.
concept_explanation.key_point: `git diff` is used in the context of code coverage, and the Python syntax focus is on the `in` operator, which checks whether a specific item is included in the list of changes.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that if parts of a string are similar, the result is True. List membership checks whether there is an element with the exact same value as the entire item.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there are no duplicate items in the list, the result is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The search string `debug=True` appears exactly once in the list. Therefore, the membership test returns True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `in` returns `True` if the same value exists within the collection.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The second item in the list exactly matches the search string.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the actual items in the list were not checked all the way to the end.

answer_explanation.takeaway: If you structure the diff check, you can read it in the order of **value to find → search the list → boolean result**.

title: Check if there are any uncommitted changes to the restore target
reading_goal: Check whether the target path exists in the modified list to assess the risk of data loss.
code:
modified_files = ["src/pwa/app.js", "README.md"]
target = "src/pwa/app.js"
would_discard_changes = target in modified_files
question: When `would_discard_changes` is True, what is the most important thing to watch out for before restoring?
choices: Uncommitted changes to app.js may be lost
The browser cache is completely cleared.
answer: Uncommitted changes to app.js may be lost
explanation: Since the target path is inside `modified_files`, it is still represented as a modified file. This is because `restore` can undo these changes, so you must first verify the risk of losing necessary modifications. A common source of confusion: “The remote repository is automatically deleted.” The primary risk of `restore` is the loss of changes in the current working tree, not the deletion of the remote repository. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when users confuse changes in the local working tree with the behavior of the remote repository. Before performing any `restore`-related operations, first verify the **current modified status of the target file**.
project_context: This ties into the workflow of first checking the state of the working tree to ensure that even when using `restore` after an incorrect patch, any necessary local modifications are not lost.
reading_goal_internal: restore 대상 경로가 modified 목록에 존재하는지 확인해 작업 손실 위험을 해석한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `value in container` is a membership test that checks whether a specific value is present in a container.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Compare the file path on the left with the modified list on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: If the target file is in a "modified" state before the "restore" operation, be aware that changes not yet committed to the repository may be lost.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think of `restore` simply as a command to fetch the latest file remotely. Here, the key is to understand the risks involved in reverting changes to the working tree.

teaching_example.code:
modified = ["app.py", "README.md"]
target = "app.py"
risky = target in modified
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since app.py is on the modified list, `risky` is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since the target path is inside `modified_files`, it is still treated as a modified file.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the `restore` function can undo these changes, you must first verify that there is no risk of losing necessary modifications.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The primary risk of `restore` is the loss of changes to the current working tree, not the deletion of the remote repository.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the learner confused changes to the local working tree with the behavior of the remote repository.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Before performing any operations in the `restore` series, first check the **current modification status of the target file**.

title: Creating a new feature branch and switching to the current branch
reading_goal: Read the state changes resulting from a method call that creates a branch and changes the current branch simultaneously.
question: What is the value of ``repo.current_branch`` after the call?
explanation: The branch name passed to `switch_create` is stored in `current_branch` within the method. This is because the method definition executes `self.current_branch = name`. A common source of confusion: `main` is the current branch before the call and changes to a new branch after the call. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the state change following the method call is not reflected. The branch switching code should be read as **passing a new name → creating a branch → changing the current branch**.
project_context: This ties into a workflow where major changes are validated on a separate feature branch before being merged into the main branch to maintain the main branch’s stability.
reading_goal_internal: branch 생성과 current branch 변경을 함께 수행하는 method call의 상태 변화를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `obj.method(arg)` calls the object’s method while passing an argument value.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the called object, method name, and branch name being passed in that order.
concept_explanation.key_point: In this example, `switch_create` creates a new branch and immediately sets that branch as `current_branch`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to think that creating a new branch will delete the `main` branch. However, the `main` branch remains in the branch list.

teaching_example.walkthrough: feature/a is added to the list of branches, and the current branch becomes feature/a.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The branch name passed to `switch_create` is stored in `current_branch` within the method.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the method definition executes `self.current_branch = name`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `main` is the `current branch` before the call and changes to a new branch after the call.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the state change following the method call has not been reflected.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The code for switching branches reads as **pass new name → create branch → change current branch**.

title: Checking the “unresolved merge” status using a conflict marker
reading_goal: It checks for the presence of specific conflict marker strings to interpret the cause of the automatic merge failure.
code:
text = '<<<<<<< HEAD
APP_DATA_VERSION = "v32"
=======
APP_DATA_VERSION = "v33"
>>>>>>> feature'
has_conflict = "<<<<<<< HEAD" in text
question: `has_conflict` Which of the following means that `True` is correct?
choices: Git was unable to automatically determine which change to select
answer: Git was unable to automatically determine which change to select
explanation: Since the conflict marker remains in the source text, it is determined that an unresolved conflict remains. This is because Git marks two different areas of change that it could not automatically resolve as markers. A common source of confusion: “JSON validation succeeded”—the conflict marker is unrelated to the JSON validation result. Misinterpretation: This occurs when the Git merge status is confused with the data validation status. A merge conflict follows the process: **marker detection → manual selection → marker removal → revalidation**.
project_context: Several patches are linked to the workflow that identifies conflicts—using markers—when the same line in app.js is modified.
reading_goal_internal: 특정 conflict marker 문자열의 존재 여부를 검사해 자동 병합 실패 상태를 해석한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `substring in text` checks whether a specific substring is contained within a string.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Compare the left marker with the entire text on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: `<<<<<<< HEAD` If the same marker remains, it indicates a conflict where Git cannot automatically determine which change to select.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the presence of a `marker` means the merge was successful. On the contrary, it’s a signal that manual resolution is required.

teaching_example.code:
text = "<<<<<<< HEAD
a
=======
b
>>>>>>> branch"
found = "<<<<<<< HEAD" in text
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since a marker exists, `found` is True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since the "conflict marker" remains in the source text, I determine that an unresolved conflict remains.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because Git marks two different areas of change that it was unable to select automatically as markers.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The "conflict marker" is unrelated to the JSON validation results.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the Git merge status was confused with the data validation status.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "merge conflict" is described as **marker detection → manual selection → marker removal → revalidation**.

title: Reading the Pages deployment steps sequentially using a for loop
reading_goal: The `for` loop reads the flow where it binds each item from the beginning of the `deploy_steps` list to `step` one by one and executes the same body in order.
code:
deploy_steps = [
    "commit",
    "git push",
    "pages build/deploy",
    "public URL updated",
]

executed = []
for step in deploy_steps:
    executed.append(step)

print(executed[1])
question: What is the value passed to `step` in the second iteration?
explanation: 1) The first item in the list is `commit`. 2) In the first iteration of the `for` loop, the `step` is `commit`. 3) When moving to the next iteration, the second item in the list, `git push`, is selected. 4) Therefore, the `step` for the second iteration is `git push`.
project_context: This context represents, using Python data, the sequence in which local changes are pushed to a remote repository, go through the configured Pages build/deploy process, and are reflected in the public URL.
reading_goal_internal: for 문이 deploy_steps 리스트의 첫 항목부터 하나씩 step에 바인딩해 같은 본문을 순서대로 실행하는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `for step in deploy_steps:` iterates through the collection, retrieving one item at a time and assigning it to `step`, then executes the body of the loop.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After verifying the actual order of the list’s items, track the execution step by step, starting from the first item and proceeding to the current step value and the body of the code.
concept_explanation.key_point: Regardless of the domain meaning of a deployment stage, in Python **list order becomes iteration order**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that a `for` loop executes its steps in arbitrary order. However, list iteration proceeds from the beginning.

teaching_example.code:
steps = ["build", "test", "publish"]
seen = []
for step in steps:
    seen.append(step)
print(seen[0])
teaching_example.walkthrough: The first step of the first iteration is `build`, the first item in the list.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The first item in the list is `commit`. 2) In the first iteration of the `for` loop, the `step` is `commit`. 3) When moving to the next iteration, the second item in the list, `git push`, is selected. 4) Therefore, the `step` for the second iteration is `git push`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The second item in the list is `git push`, and the `for` loop iterates sequentially from the beginning.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since "Pages build/deploy" is the third item, it enters the "step" phase in the third iteration.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Let’s try to match the list index order with the iteration count on a 1:1 basis.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A `for` loop repeats the process of **binding the first item → executing the body → moving to the next item**.

title: Reading the call that uses `replace()` to convert CRLF to LF strings
reading_goal: Pass the existing CRLF and the new LF strings as arguments to the `replace` method of the string object `text`, and read the new string that is returned.
question: `text.replace("\r\n", "\n")` What value does the final comparison after the call output?
explanation:
1) The text contains two `
` characters. 2) The `replace` function returns a new string in which each `
` has been replaced with `
`. 3) That new string is stored in `normalized`. 4) Since it matches the expected string, the comparison result is `True`.
project_context: This card models a situation where line break differences can occur between the Windows working directory and Git policies using Python string normalization.
reading_goal_internal: 문자열 객체 text의 replace 메서드에 기존 CRLF와 새 LF 문자열을 인자로 전달하고 반환되는 새 문자열을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `text.replace(old, new)` is a method call that returns a new string in which all instances of “old” in the string text are replaced with “new.”
concept_explanation.how_to_read: The text to the left of the dot is the target of the call, "replace" is the method, and the first argument is the string to find, while the second is the string to replace it with.
concept_explanation.key_point: The string is not modified in place by this call; instead, **a new, converted string is returned**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that the original `text` variable automatically changes after a call. You must store the return value in a new name.

teaching_example.walkthrough: A new string, in which two CRLFs have been replaced with LF, is stored in `normalized`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step:
1) The text contains two `
` characters. 2) The `replace` function returns a new string in which each `
` has been replaced with `
`. 3) That new string is stored in `normalized`. 4) Since it matches the expected string, the comparison result is `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: replace Since the return value exactly matches the expected string, which uses only LF, the result is True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since `replace` replaces both CRLFs with LF, it matches the expected string.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the original text and the normalized text returned by `replace`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Method calls are read in the following order: **check the receiver → pass arguments → calculate the return value → check the storage location**.

title: Reading the paths of two files to be included in the same commit as a list literal
reading_goal: Read the structure where the two strings inside the square brackets form a single ordered list value, and that list is stored in `commit_files`.
question: How many items are in the `commit_files` list literal?
explanation: 1) Count the first path string. 2) Count the second path string. 3) The final comma does not create a separate value. 4) Therefore, the list length is 2.
project_context: This aligns with the design principle of grouping only the lesson JSON and app connection changes directly related to a single feature addition within the same commit scope.
reading_goal_internal: 대괄호 안 두 문자열이 순서를 가진 하나의 list 값이 되고 그 리스트가 commit_files에 저장되는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A list literal creates a single list object by directly listing values in the code, such as ``[value1, value2]``.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, locate the boundaries of the square brackets, and then count the actual value expressions—separated by commas—from the left within them.
concept_explanation.key_point: The two file paths are **two items contained within a single `commit_files` list**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to count this as three items because of the final trailing comma. A trailing comma does not create a new item.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there are two actual value expressions, the list length is 2.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Count the first path string. 2) Count the second path string. 3) The final comma does not create a separate value. 4) Therefore, the list length is 2.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since there are two actual path values inside the list literal, the correct answer is 2.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The final trailing comma does not refer to the third item.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Count the number of actual value expressions instead of the number of commas.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A list literal **creates a single list by containing the actual values inside square brackets in order**.

title: Check whether the temporary script remains in the untracked list using `in`
reading_goal: It checks whether the name of the temporary file on the left matches one of the items in the untracked list on the right and reads the Boolean result.
code:
temp_script = "python_reading_trainer_expand_v33_git_github_workflow.ps1"
untracked = ["notes.txt", "debug.log"]

still_present = temp_script in untracked
print(still_present)
question: What is the result of `temp_script in untracked`?
explanation: 1) The value being searched for is a long ps1 filename. 2) It is different from the first entry in “untracked,” notes.txt. 3) It is also different from the second entry, debug.log. 4) Since no matching entry was found, the result of `in` is False.
project_context: It is integrated into a Git workflow that checks for any unexpected untracked files after cleaning up temporary patch files.
reading_goal_internal: 왼쪽 임시 파일 이름이 오른쪽 untracked 리스트의 항목 중 하나와 같은지 확인해 Boolean 결과를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `value in collection` Returns True if the left-hand value is contained within the right-hand collection, and False otherwise.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the actual string in `temp_script` and all items in the `untracked` list, then look for any matching values.
concept_explanation.key_point: In Python code reading, the **membership result—whether a value remains in the current list—** is more critical than the deletion operation itself.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `in` It’s easy to assume that this part returns True even if only part of the filename matches, as with a string. In a list, it looks for the exact match.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since there is a list item such as `patch.ps1`, the result is `True`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The value being searched for is a long ps1 filename. 2) It is different from the first entry in “untracked,” notes.txt. 3) It is also different from the second entry, debug.log. 4) Since no matching entry was found, the result of `in` is False.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since there is no item in the untracked list that matches `temp_script`, the membership result is False.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: There are no values in the list that match the filename of the ps1 file.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It compares the search value with each entire item in the list, rather than with a substring.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `in` is interpreted as **checking for a value → comparing it to collection items → True if found, False if not found**.

title: Compare whether the SHA of `local main` matches that of `origin/main` using `==`
reading_goal: Check the SHA strings referred to by the two names and read whether `==` produces True when they are the same string.
code:
local_main = "a1b2c3d"
origin_main = "a1b2c3d"

same_recorded_commit = local_main == origin_main
print(same_recorded_commit)
question: What is the result of `local_main == origin_main`?
explanation: 1) `local_main` is `a1b2c3d`. 2) `origin_main` is also `a1b2c3d`. 3) The contents of the two strings are identical. 4) Therefore, the result of `==` is `True`.
project_context: This relates to the context in which `git status`’s “up to date with origin/main” is interpreted as a match between the local `main` branch and the commit recorded in the local remote-tracking ref.
reading_goal_internal: 두 이름이 가리키는 SHA 문자열을 확인하고 `==`가 동일한 문자열이면 True를 만드는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `a == b` is a comparison expression that returns True or False depending on whether two values are equal.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check the current string values of `local_main` and `origin_main`, and then compare them to see if their contents match.
concept_explanation.key_point: The fact that this comparison evaluates to True means **the two values currently stored in the code are the same**; it does not mean that the remote server was queried in real time.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If the two SHAs match, it’s easy to jump to the conclusion that the code has just been updated to the latest version on the GitHub server.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the contents of the two strings are identical, the == comparison evaluates to True.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `local_main` is `a1b2c3d`. 2) `origin_main` is also `a1b2c3d`. 3) The contents of the two strings are identical. 4) Therefore, the result of `==` is `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since the two SHA strings are exactly the same, the result of the equality comparison is True.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Since there are no other characters between the two strings, the program will not determine that they are different.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It distinguishes between the fact that the variable names are different and whether the actual values stored in the variables are the same.

answer_explanation.takeaway: `==` is read in the following order: **check current values on both sides → compare value equality → generate a Boolean result**.
